hook: SCP-096 is built around a single trigger, and the article makes sure you understand how easy it is to set off. The most memorable part isn't the description but the interview at the end: the voice of someone who was there, and the one small moment that kept him alive. That interview is profane and describes soldiers being torn apart in plain terms.
whyItMatters:
096 is a textbook rule-based anomaly, defined less by what it is than by the condition that sets it off. A premise you can explain in one sentence is easy to retell, which goes a long way toward explaining why this file is so widely known.

It also shows how bureaucracy can become part of the story. A termination request moves from petition to approval within a few lines, and the outcome is handed off to an incident report that the article never includes.
thingsToNotice:
The trigger is seeing its face, by any means: in person, on video or in a single photograph. The creature then covers its face, screams and weeps, and a minute or two later sprints toward whoever looked, wherever they are, at speeds nothing has managed to stop; when it arrives it kills them, the rest is expunged, and no victim has ever left a trace. That is why the procedures ban cameras rather than weapons, and why the brief note that drawings don't set it off matters later.

The interview supplies what the clinical sections refuse to. The captain's squad saw the face because it turned while he happened to look away to take a call from a doctor; it then ripped a corporal's leg off, shrugged off roughly a thousand rounds, and kept tearing his men apart with half its torso blown away by an anti-tank launcher. Only once his squad was dead did the backup team get a bag over its head, at which point it simply sat down. When he is offered an artist's drawing of the face at the end, he refuses, and the doctor's very next act is to request its termination.
